initial_observation.demographics: An 80-year-old man with a medical history of glaucoma, hypertension and first degree heart block
initial_observation.encounter_context: presented with a 3-month history of frontal headaches, initially seen by his general practitioner
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Presented with frontal headaches; routine CT head showed no intracranial masses or bony lesions but an incidental mature lacunar infarct of the left ventral thalamus; no radiographic cause determined for headaches; developed bilateral jaw pain with claudication; initially diagnosed with bruxism by dentist

evidence_items.source_text: A routine CT head was requested by his general practitioner (GP). This showed no intracranial masses or bony lesions but incidentally revealed a mature lacunar infarct of the left ventral thalamus. There was no radiographic cause determined for his headaches.

Three days after the CT scan (3 months after initial presentation to healthcare), the patient visited ophthalmology for a routine glaucoma follow-up appointment. The ophthalmologist elicited episodes of diplopia, amaurosis fugax and significant weight loss in the preceding months. There was no history of scalp tenderness, fever or proximal muscle pain and stiffness. Examination revealed bilateral tender, nodular and weakly pulsatile temporal arteries. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect or anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Inflammatory markers were not significantly raised: C-reactive protein (CRP) 11 mg/L (<10) and ESR 15 mm/hour (1–19).
Temporal and axillary artery ultrasound (US) demonstrated a characteristic positive halo sign in the right temporal artery (figure 1).
A right temporal artery biopsy (TAB) revealed a muscular artery with focal adventitial chronic inflammation and intimal hyperplasia with mild inflammation (figure 2), consistent with GCA.
Sixty milligrams of prednisolone was initiated due to the presence of jaw claudication and visual symptoms in accordance with the British Society of Rheumatology guidelines.
At 4-week follow-up, his symptoms improved significantly and inflammatory markers remained low (CRP <3, ESR 2).

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: In light of the ongoing headaches, jaw claudication, diplopia, amaurosis fugax and weight loss, a diagnosis of GCA was suspected.
Recognising that normal inflammatory markers do not rule out GCA, rheumatologists arranged urgent investigation.
Temporal and axillary artery ultrasound (US) demonstrated a characteristic positive halo sign in the right temporal artery (figure 1).
A right temporal artery biopsy (TAB) revealed a muscular artery with focal adventitial chronic inflammation and intimal hyperplasia with mild inflammation (figure 2), consistent with GCA.
